<reason>Both sides were sharp and stayed on the motion, and the exchange narrowed cleanly to two questions: is the guarantee enforceable given upstream licensing, and is flipping the default fair to buyers who never wanted heritability. CON's best work was the heritable-vs-personal contract distinction (gym memberships, non-assignable tenancies against PRO's lease/stock/cemetery-plot list) and the elegant closing dilemma that PRO's rule either evaporates where sublicenses are personal or becomes CON's own priced tier with a flipped default. PRO, however, gave a genuinely responsive answer to that dilemma that CON never neutralized: voiding non-transferability in anything sold as a "purchase" forces storefronts either to acquire heritable rights upstream or to stop charging purchase prices, which is bargaining pressure disclosure alone cannot generate. PRO also defused CON's bankruptcy attack with the unrebutted insolvency analogy (no lease, gift card, or pension survives insolvency intact, and we do not refuse to create rights for that reason), and handled the three-children mechanic more cleanly via ordinary probate allocation of indivisible assets. PRO's weighing frame — who bears the cost of an unnegotiated term, and why no seller will voluntarily sell what he currently gets back for free — carried more decisional force than CON's residual harms (a modest price effect mitigated by PRO's own opt-out, plus the sudden-death privacy point, which PRO did drop in closing and which is CON's cleanest surviving sting). Net: CON was more incisive line by line and owned the last word, but the core CON horn depends on an asserted claim that all publishers would refuse heritability, which PRO undercut by showing heritability's only real cost is a foregone second sale while refusing it forfeits purchase-price revenue entirely.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing [B5.4] answering CON's "your rule collapses into honest labeling": voiding non-transferability means the storefront must buy heritable rights upstream or stop charging purchase prices, which is bargaining pressure aimed at rightsholders that disclosure never generates. CON's closing re-asserted the collapse framing without engaging that mechanism. Runner-up: CON's [A2.2] showing PRO's inheritable-claims list was all sold as heritable, contrasted with personal, non-assignable contracts.</best_rebuttal>
